rv.q: In "Smokey Joe's Cafe," the songs have been enshrined as theater and they can't hold up under the weight of all that attention in such a formal setting.
The music itself, even if it doesn't have much emotional range or variety, is wildly infectious, particularly the way it's sung by the sensationally talented cast.

cn.t: Critics find this Leiber and Stoller song revue breezy and bouncy, but question whether these jukebox hits translate effectively to the Broadway stage, where they struggle under the weight of theatrical presentation.

sg.ra: August Wilson has no traditional proscenium arch and a 38-ft-wide stage opening that ends at the side walls, so mid-center orchestra rows D-G pick up the full width no other Broadway house exposes; the lower stage (which extends over the usual pit area) also means you are not losing actors' feet here the way you would in a standard proscenium house. Rows E-G sit ahead of the mezzanine overhang line (row L) so nothing is cropped overhead.

August Wilson's mezzanine is the house's only elevated level (no balcony above it), so front-mezz row A looks straight down onto the low, pit-extended stage with nothing overhead - an unusually clean overhead angle you cannot get in the three-tier houses across 52nd. Row A is also the one mezz row noted for better legroom in this otherwise tight-rowed house, and it sits well forward of the overhang start at row L.

Because August Wilson is a single-balcony house, the mezzanine keeps an effective rake all the way back and is not shadowed by an upper level the way multi-tier Shubert houses are. Mid-center rows D-H stay ahead of where the overhang would cut the top of the stage (the overhang affects the orchestra below from row L onward, not the mezz itself), and row H is specifically cited for extra legroom plus elevation over the row in front - unusual in this tight-legroom house. Forum consensus on BWW and TripAdvisor repeatedly recommends mezz over mid/rear orchestra at the same price.

August Wilson's front sides are flanked by Roman arches and decorative columns (a feature unique to this 1925 Crane/Franzheim house) - they don't block views but they physically frame side orchestra wings, and the 38-ft-wide proscenium-less opening means side seats can still see stage-width action the way they can't in narrower houses. Front-row sides (A-C) feel uncomfortably close; mid-side D-G is the workable band.

The August Wilson mezzanine overhang begins at row L and by rows V-ZZ it cuts off the top of the stage - a specific cutoff repeatedly confirmed by SeatPlan, Headout, and the Tripadvisor forum Q&A about row P. Because this is a single-balcony house the overhang is deep and low, and a BWW forum poster who sat Orch row W for Jersey Boys confirmed losing overhead projections. For the same price, front-to-mid mezzanine always wins here.

August Wilson's mezz tops out at row Q (it skips row I) and there is no balcony above it, so rear mezz is physically the back wall of the house. SeatPlan calls rear mezz up to row M 'impressively good' value, but beyond M you're at the back wall of a 1,239-seat house with no upper level to compare against; sightlines remain unobstructed thanks to the effective rake but binoculars help for intimate dramas. Tight legroom here since row H's legroom bump does not apply this far back.
